summary: Specifies a Cisco Systems extension to the IPFIX information model from RFC 5102 for exporting application information. It describes vendor-specific fields. It is informational and not an Internet Standards Track specification.

eli5.summary: Network devices can report what traffic passes by. This memo describes extra fields one company added so reports can also say which application the traffic belongs to.

questions: how to export application names in ipfix
what is application identification in ipfix
how do operators monitor application usage
what is a classification engine id
subtitle: Application identification in IP flow exports with Cisco extensions.

tldr.problem: Network operators need visibility into what applications are running on their networks, but the standard IPFIX flow export format does not provide a way to export application identification.
tldr.mechanism: This memo specifies a Cisco extension to IPFIX that adds an applicationId field, composed of a classification engine ID and a selector ID, along with additional fields to name and categorize applications.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now export detailed application information alongside flow statistics, enabling application-aware analytics, QoS, and security policies.

today: RFC 6759 is an Informational memo documenting a Cisco Systems extension to IPFIX. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference for implementing application-aware flow export.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network administrators need visibility into what traffic is flowing across their networks. The IPFIX protocol already exports information about flows (connections between devices), but it does not identify which application created each flow. Application identification is important for understanding network usage patterns, enforcing security policies, and managing quality of service.

Network devices use various methods to identify applications. They may examine source and destination ports (layer 4), look at protocol headers (layer 7), inspect packet contents, or analyze traffic behavior patterns. Some applications deliberately hide on non-standard ports or use encryption, so accurate identification requires sophisticated analysis.
sections.eli5: Network operators want to know which apps are using the network, not just which computers. This memo explains how to send that information in a standard format.

sections.title: The applicationId Field
sections.content:
The core of this specification is the applicationId information element, a single field that identifies an application in two parts. The first 8 bits contain a classification engine ID, which identifies the registry being used. The remaining bits contain a selector ID, which identifies the application within that registry.

This design allows multiple registries to coexist. For example, one registry might contain standardized IANA protocol numbers (layer 3 protocols), while another contains enterprise-proprietary layer 7 application definitions. The classification engine ID tells the collector which registry to consult.
sections.eli5: Think of applicationId like a two-part code: the first part says which book to look in, and the second part says which page number in that book.

sections.title: Classification Engines
sections.content:
This memo defines multiple classification engines for different types of application identification. IANA-L3 (ID 1) uses standardized Internet protocol numbers for layer 3 protocols like ICMP. IANA-L4 (ID 3) uses IANA well-known port numbers for layer 4 services like SNMP. PANA-L7 (ID 13) allows enterprises to define their own layer 7 application registries, such as Webex or custom proprietary applications.

Additional engines support layer 2 protocols (ETHERTYPE, LLC), proprietary layer 3 and 4 definitions, user-defined applications, and a special engine (PANA-L7-PEN) that includes a Private Enterprise Number to identify which organization owns the application registry. This flexibility lets operators use global standard registries where they exist and local registries where needed.
sections.eli5: Different companies and organizations keep different lists of what applications are. This system lets network equipment consult the right list for each type of application.

sections.title: Exporting Application Information
sections.content:
IPFIX exporters include the applicationId in flow records alongside existing statistics like byte counts and packet counts. For applications that use locally unique identifiers (those that differ per router), or for proprietary registries, the exporter sends an options template record that maps application IDs to application names and descriptions.

This memo also specifies additional information elements to categorize applications into categories (browsing, email, gaming), subcategories (streaming video, social media), and groups (all FTP variants). Boolean fields indicate whether an application uses peer-to-peer technology, tunneling, or encryption. This metadata helps operators apply consistent policies based on application type.
sections.eli5: Along with the traffic data, equipment sends a separate message that explains what each application code means, like a legend for a map.

sections.title: Use Cases and Deployment
sections.content:
Network operators use application visibility for several purposes. Visibility and analytics help understand network usage trends and identify heavy consumers. Security functions leverage application knowledge for application-based firewalls, URL filtering, parental controls, and intrusion detection. Quality of service policies prioritize or deprioritize applications based on business needs.

The specification is vendor-specific (published by Cisco), but the extension mechanisms and general approach have been influential in the industry. Implementation requires sophisticated metering processes that can detect applications through port analysis, content inspection, and behavioral analysis. The use of multiple classification engines ensures the mechanism can grow to support new application identification methods.
sections.eli5: Once network operators know which apps are running, they can make smarter decisions: which traffic gets priority, which is risky, and what the network is used for.

items.label: IANA-L3
items.desc: IP protocol numbers (IPv4, TCP, UDP, ICMP)

items.label: IANA-L4
items.desc: Well-known TCP/UDP port numbers (HTTP, SMTP, DNS)
